title: Greece and Persia
description: An illustrated map of the Greek city-states and the Persian empire, from Olympia and the rise of Cyrus through Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis, Athens and Sparta, to Alexander’s conquest of Persia, and the first marathon and the digging of Persepolis.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of Greece and Persia, from about 776 BCE to today
note: Based mainly on Greek historians (Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Arrian and Plutarch), on Persian and Babylonian inscriptions and tablets, and on excavated sites; each chapter says which it follows. The Greek writers were not neutral, and their numbers for Persian armies are much too large. Native names are given in Latin letters. The map is stylised and not to scale. Delphi, Thermopylae, Marathon, Salamis and Pasargadae are drawn a little apart from their true spots so their pins don’t overlap. Coasts are drawn as they are today; at Thermopylae and Miletus the sea once came much further inland. Lands under Powers are painted loosely.

steps.title: Games at Olympia
steps.text: Later Greek writers date the first games at Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus, to 776 BCE, from a list drawn up about 400 BCE. Every four years men from rival cities gather under a sacred truce to run, wrestle and box. Shared games, gods and language make the Greeks one people, though never one state.
steps.today: Today: Archaia Olympia, in the western Peloponnese, Greece. The flame for each Olympic Games is still lit here.

steps.title: The oracle and the colonies
steps.text: At Delphi the priestess of Apollo, the Pythia, answers questions in the god’s name. Cities ask her blessing before sending out settlers, and Greek colonies spread from Marseille (Massalia) to Byzantium and the shores of the Black Sea. There are hundreds of Greek city-states (poleis), each with its own laws, army and festivals.
steps.today: Today: beside the town of Delfi, Greece; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Thinkers of Ionia
steps.text: Miletus is the richest Ionian Greek city on the coast of Asia. Herodotus says Thales of Miletus foretold an eclipse that halted a battle of Lydians and Medes, dated to 585 BCE. Thales and his pupil Anaximander look for natural causes, not the whims of gods; Anaximander is said to have drawn the first Greek map of the world.
steps.today: Today: ruins near Balat, Aydın province, Turkey. Silt from the Maeander river has pushed the sea kilometres away.

steps.title: Cyrus, king of Persia
steps.text: Cyrus, king of Anshan in Persia (Pars), rebels against his overlord, Astyages, king of the Medes. A Babylonian chronicle says Astyages’ own army seized him and handed him to Cyrus, who takes the Median capital, Ecbatana. At Pasargadae Cyrus builds palaces in walled gardens. His family, the Achaemenids, will rule the largest empire yet seen.
steps.today: Today: Pasargadae, Fars province, Iran; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Croesus and the oracle
steps.text: Croesus of Lydia, famed for his gold, rules from Sardis. Herodotus says he asked Delphi whether to attack Persia and was told he would destroy a great empire. He crosses the Halys river, and the empire he destroys is his own: Cyrus takes Sardis, and soon the Ionian Greek cities. The Lydians are credited with the first coins.
steps.today: Today: Sart, near Salihli, Manisa province, Turkey.

steps.title: Babylon, Egypt and a tomb
steps.text: In 539 BCE Cyrus takes Babylon, by his own account without a fight. He dies in 530 BCE; Herodotus says in battle with Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae, though other writers disagree, and he is buried in a stone tomb at Pasargadae. His son Cambyses takes Egypt in 525 BCE. Persia now rules from the Aegean to Central Asia.
steps.today: Today: Babylon is near Hillah, Iraq. Cyrus’s tomb still stands at Pasargadae.

steps.title: Darius tells his story
steps.text: In 522 BCE Cambyses dies while a man ruling as his brother Bardiya holds the throne. Darius and six nobles kill him; Darius says he was an impostor, a priest named Gaumata, and many historians doubt it. Darius crushes revolts across the empire and has his victories carved high on a cliff at Behistun, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian.
steps.today: Today: Bisotun, near Kermanshah, Iran; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: A palace for all lands
steps.text: Darius begins a great terrace of palaces at Persepolis. On the stairways of the audience hall (apadana), carved envoys of 23 subject peoples, among them Ionians, Babylonians, Egyptians, Bactrians and Indians, bring gifts to the king. Clay tablets from its walls record rations paid to workers, men and women, with extra for new mothers.
steps.today: Today: Takht-e Jamshid, near Marvdasht, Fars province, Iran; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The Royal Road
steps.text: Herodotus describes a royal road from Sardis to Susa, some 2,500 km, with 111 staging posts: three months on foot. Royal couriers ride it in relays, a fresh horse and rider for each day’s stage. His line that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stops them is carved on a New York post office.
steps.today: Today: Shush, Khuzestan province, Iran; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Down the Indus
steps.text: Herodotus says Darius sent a Greek sea captain, Scylax of Caryanda, down the Indus to the sea and then west, reaching Egypt in the thirtieth month, before conquering the Indians. Darius lists Gandhara and Hindush, the Indus lands, among his peoples, and Herodotus says the Indians paid the largest tribute of all: 360 talents of gold dust.
steps.today: Today: the Indus delta, Sindh, Pakistan.

steps.title: A bridge to Europe
steps.text: Darius marches against the Scythians, horse-riding nomads north of the Black Sea. Mandrocles, an engineer from Samos, bridges the Bosporus with boats, and Ionian Greeks build and guard another over the Danube. The Scythians retreat, burning the grass, and Darius turns back. Thrace becomes Persian, and Macedon’s king gives earth and water, the sign of submission.
steps.today: Today: Istanbul, Turkey, where bridges and tunnels now cross the Bosporus.

steps.title: Rule by the people
steps.text: After the tyrant Hippias is driven out, Cleisthenes reorganises Athens into ten new tribes and a Council of 500 drawn from every village. The assembly of citizens decides; this rule by the people (demokratia) includes only free adult men. Fearing Sparta, Athens sends envoys to the Persian governor at Sardis, who give earth and water; Athens later disowns them.
steps.today: Today: the Pnyx hill, where the assembly met, faces the Acropolis in Athens.

steps.title: The Ionian Revolt
steps.text: Aristagoras, ruler of Miletus, leads the Ionian cities against Persia. Sparta refuses to help; Athens sends 20 ships and Eretria five, and in 498 BCE they burn Sardis. Persia strikes back, defeats the Ionian fleet off the island of Lade and sacks Miletus in 494 BCE. Herodotus says the survivors were sent to live near the mouth of the Tigris.
steps.today: Today: Lade is no longer an island; silt has joined it to the mainland.

steps.title: Marathon
steps.text: A Persian fleet under Datis and Artaphernes burns Eretria and lands at Marathon, guided by the exiled Hippias. Athens sends the runner Pheidippides to Sparta, but the Spartans wait for the full moon. Athenians and Plataeans, perhaps 10,000 men, charge and win. Herodotus counts 6,400 Persian dead and 192 Athenians, buried under a mound that still stands.
steps.today: Today: the burial mound (Soros) at Marathon, north-east of Athens.

steps.title: Silver for ships
steps.text: Miners at Laurion, in the south of Attica, strike a rich vein of silver. Rather than share it out, Themistocles persuades the Athenians to build warships: 200, says Herodotus. Each trireme carries about 170 rowers in three banks, mostly poorer citizens, who gain a new voice in the democracy. The silver also strikes Athens’ owl coins.
steps.today: Today: Lavrio, Attica, Greece, where ancient shafts and ore-washing floors can still be seen.

steps.title: Xerxes crosses
steps.text: Darius dies in 486 BCE, and his son Xerxes leads the invasion himself. Engineers bridge the Hellespont with boats; when a storm wrecks the first bridges, Herodotus says, Xerxes has the sea whipped. A canal is dug through the Athos peninsula for his fleet. Herodotus gives his army as 1.7 million; modern estimates are far lower and disputed.
steps.today: Today: the Dardanelles, Turkey. Surveys at Athos have traced Xerxes’ canal.

steps.title: Thermopylae
steps.text: The Spartan king Leonidas holds the narrow pass at Thermopylae with some 7,000 Greeks, among them 300 Spartans. For two days the Persians cannot break through. Then a local man, Ephialtes, shows them a mountain path. Leonidas sends most of the Greeks away and dies fighting with those who stay. At sea, the Greek fleet fights off Artemisium.
steps.today: Today: the coast has moved kilometres from the pass; a monument to Leonidas stands by the road.

steps.title: Salamis
steps.text: Athens is emptied, and the Persians burn the Acropolis. Themistocles lures the Persian fleet into the narrow strait off Salamis, where the Greek triremes, fewer but in home waters, ram and sink their ships while Xerxes watches from the shore. Queen Artemisia of Halicarnassus commands ships on his side. Xerxes returns to Asia, leaving his general Mardonius.
steps.today: Today: the island of Salamina, west of Piraeus, Greece.

steps.title: Plataea and Mycale
steps.text: The largest Greek army yet, led by the Spartan regent Pausanias, defeats the Persians at Plataea, and Mardonius is killed. Herodotus says that on the same day a Greek fleet burns the Persian ships at Mycale, near Miletus, and the Ionians rise again. The victors set up a bronze column of twisted snakes at Delphi, inscribed with 31 Greek states.
steps.today: Today: the Serpent Column, without its heads, stands in the old Hippodrome of Istanbul.

steps.title: The Delian League
steps.text: Athens leads a league of island and coastal cities to free the Greeks of Asia and keep Persia out, with its treasury on Apollo’s sacred island of Delos. Members pay in ships or silver. When Naxos tries to leave, Athens forces it back, and in 454 BCE the treasury moves to Athens. The league has become an Athenian empire.
steps.today: Today: Delos, near Mykonos, is uninhabited: an open-air museum and a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The Parthenon
steps.text: In 472 BCE Aeschylus’ play The Persians, the oldest Greek play that survives, shows Salamis through the eyes of Xerxes’ court. Pericles leads Athens from about 461 BCE and, from 447 BCE, rebuilds the temples the Persians burnt, partly with the league’s money. The Parthenon, finished by 432 BCE, houses Phidias’ gold and ivory statue of Athena.
steps.today: Today: the Acropolis of Athens, a World Heritage Site. Many Parthenon sculptures are in the British Museum, London; Greece asks for their return.

steps.title: Persian gold, Spartan victory
steps.text: War breaks out between Athens and Sparta in 431 BCE. Plague kills Pericles and many Athenians, and in 413 BCE an Athenian army is lost in Sicily. Persia now pays for a Spartan fleet, and the Persian prince Cyrus the Younger funds its admiral Lysander. He captures Athens’ last fleet at Aegospotami, and Athens surrenders in 404 BCE.
steps.today: Today: modern Sparti stands beside the scant ruins. Thucydides foresaw that they would make later people doubt Sparta’s power.

steps.title: The Ten Thousand
steps.text: Cyrus the Younger hires over 10,000 Greek soldiers and marches against his brother, King Artaxerxes II. At Cunaxa, near Babylon, the Greeks win their part of the battle but Cyrus is killed. Their generals are seized and killed, and the Athenian Xenophon helps lead them north through mountains and snow. Seeing the Black Sea, they shout, “The sea! The sea!”
steps.today: Today: Trapezus is Trabzon, Turkey. Xenophon’s account of the march is the Anabasis.

steps.title: Mausolus and his tomb
steps.text: In the King’s Peace of 387 BCE, Sparta hands the Greek cities of Asia back to Persia. Mausolus, the Persian governor (satrap) of Caria, rules almost as a king from Halicarnassus. His tomb, finished after his death by his sister and widow Artemisia, joins Greek sculpture to eastern forms. One of the Seven Wonders, it gives us the word mausoleum.
steps.today: Today: Bodrum, Turkey. Crusader knights reused its stones in their castle; many of its sculptures are in the British Museum.

steps.title: Philip of Macedon
steps.text: Philip II turns Macedon, on the northern edge of the Greek world, into its strongest power, with foot soldiers armed with long pikes (sarissas). Aristotle teaches his son Alexander. In 338 BCE Philip defeats Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea and leads a league of Greek states against Persia, but in 336 BCE he is murdered in the theatre at Aigai.
steps.today: Today: Vergina, Greece. Manolis Andronikos found royal tombs here in 1977; one is often said to be Philip’s, though this is debated.

steps.title: The Granicus
steps.text: Alexander, aged 21, crosses the Hellespont with an army ancient writers put at about 37,000; at Troy he is said to honour the tomb of Achilles. At the Granicus river he charges across into the cavalry of the Persian governors and wins. Sardis surrenders, and the Ionian cities are freed; Miletus and Halicarnassus resist and fall to sieges.
steps.today: Today: the Biga river, Çanakkale province, Turkey.

steps.title: Issus
steps.text: Darius III comes west himself with a great army, but meets Alexander on narrow ground between the mountains and the sea at Issus. Alexander drives his cavalry at the king, and Darius flees, leaving his mother, wife and children in the camp. Alexander treats them with honour. A famous mosaic from Pompeii shows the two kings face to face.
steps.today: Today: near Dörtyol, Hatay province, Turkey. The Alexander Mosaic is in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples.

steps.title: Gaugamela
steps.text: After taking Tyre and Egypt, Alexander meets Darius again on open ground near Arbela. Darius has scythed chariots and elephants, but Alexander breaks through and Darius flees east once more. A Babylonian astronomer’s diary records the battle and the defeat of the Persian king’s army. Babylon and Susa open their gates, and their treasuries pay Alexander’s army.
steps.today: Today: near Erbil, Kurdistan Region, Iraq; the exact battlefield is debated.

steps.title: Persepolis burns
steps.text: Alexander forces the Persian Gates, a mountain pass, and takes Persepolis. Plutarch says its treasure needed 10,000 pairs of mules and 5,000 camels to carry. Months later the palaces burn. Ancient writers disagree whether it was planned revenge for Xerxes’ burning of Athens or a drunken feast urged on by Thais of Athens; Alexander is said to have regretted it.
steps.today: Today: excavators found the burnt layers of the treasury and the great halls.

steps.title: The last Achaemenid
steps.text: Darius flees from Ecbatana to the east, where Bessus, governor of Bactria, has him stabbed and claims the throne. Alexander finds the king dead near Hecatompylos and sends his body to Persepolis for a royal burial. After two hard years in Bactria and Sogdiana he marries Roxana, a Bactrian noble’s daughter, and in 327 BCE turns towards India.
steps.today: Today: Balkh, northern Afghanistan. For Alexander in India, see the Nanda Dynasty story.

steps.title: The weddings at Susa
steps.text: Back from India through the Gedrosian desert, Alexander holds a mass wedding at Susa. He marries Stateira, Darius’s daughter, and Parysatis, daughter of an earlier king, and about 80 of his officers marry Persian and Median noblewomen. Arrian says some 10,000 soldiers’ marriages to Asian women were recorded. Thirty thousand young Persians are trained to fight as Macedonians.
steps.today: Today: Shush, Khuzestan province, Iran. Darius’s palace at Susa has been excavated since the 1800s.

steps.title: Death in Babylon
steps.text: Alexander dies in Nebuchadnezzar’s palace at Babylon, aged 32, after days of fever; a Babylonian astronomical diary notes simply that the king died. Poison, malaria and typhoid have all been suggested. His generals divide the empire and fight for decades. Ptolemy takes Egypt, and Seleucus most of Persia’s old lands, where Greek and Persian ways mix for centuries.
steps.today: Today: near Hillah, Iraq. Seleucus later makes a treaty with Chandragupta; see the Maurya Empire story.

steps.title: The first marathon
steps.text: When the Olympic Games are revived in Athens in 1896, the scholar Michel Bréal suggests a race from Marathon to Athens, after a late legend of a messenger who ran with news of the victory and died. Herodotus tells only of the run to Sparta. Spyridon Louis, a Greek water-carrier, wins in just under three hours.
steps.today: Today: the Athens Marathon follows the route every November.

steps.title: Digging Persepolis
steps.text: Archaeologists from the University of Chicago’s Oriental Institute, led by Ernst Herzfeld and then Erich Schmidt, clear the terrace at Persepolis. In 1933 they find tens of thousands of clay tablets in its walls, most in Elamite: the empire’s own records of rations, travel and work. Lent to Chicago for study in 1936, many have since been returned to Iran.
steps.today: Today: Persepolis is a World Heritage Site, and work on the tablets continues in Chicago and Iran.

items.name: Croesus
items.text: Croesus was so rich that “as rich as Croesus” is still a saying. He sent rich gifts to Delphi and helped pay for the great temple of Artemis at Ephesus. Herodotus tells of Solon warning him that no one should be called happy until he is dead, and of Cyrus sparing him on the pyre; both stories are probably legend.

items.name: Cyrus II, the Great
items.text: Cyrus took the lands of the Medes, Lydia and Babylon in about twenty years. Greek writers admired him: Xenophon wrote a book about his education. The Bible’s book of Isaiah calls him the Lord’s anointed, for letting Judeans go home from Babylon. His clay cylinder is sometimes called the first charter of human rights, a claim historians dispute.

items.name: Darius I
items.text: Darius divided the empire into provinces (satrapies) with fixed tribute, struck a gold coin (the daric) and linked his lands with roads and royal couriers. He built Persepolis and a palace at Susa, and finished a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea. His tomb is cut into the cliff at Naqsh-e Rostam, near Persepolis.

items.name: Miltiades
items.text: Miltiades ruled the Gallipoli peninsula under Persia, and Herodotus says he urged the Ionians to break Darius’s Danube bridge and strand the king. He fled to Athens during the Ionian Revolt and was a leading general at Marathon. A year later a failed attack on the island of Paros ended in a heavy fine, and he died of a wound.

items.name: Pheidippides
items.text: Herodotus says Pheidippides, a professional runner, reached Sparta, about 240 km away, the day after he left Athens, and met the god Pan on the way. Later writers tell of a runner who carried news of the victory from Marathon to Athens and died; Plutarch names him Thersippus or Eucles. The Spartathlon race follows Pheidippides’ road.

items.name: Themistocles
items.text: Themistocles built Athens’ navy and set the trap at Salamis, sending a slave, Sicinnus, to tell Xerxes the Greeks were about to flee. Later ostracised, voted into exile by his fellow citizens, he ended his life in the service of the Persian king, as governor of Magnesia in Asia Minor. Thucydides admired his foresight.

items.name: Xerxes I
items.text: Xerxes put down revolts in Egypt and Babylon before invading Greece. After 479 BCE he stayed in Persia, adding the Gate of All Nations and a great hall to Persepolis. He was murdered in his palace in 465 BCE. He is usually identified with Ahasuerus in the Bible’s book of Esther.

items.name: Leonidas I
items.text: One of Sparta’s two kings, Leonidas took to the pass, says Herodotus, only men who had living sons. Told to hand over his weapons, he answered, Plutarch says, “Come and take them” (molon labe). The poet Simonides wrote the Spartans’ epitaph: “Stranger, tell the Spartans that we lie here, obedient to their words.”

items.name: Artemisia I
items.text: Ruling Halicarnassus under Persia, Artemisia brought five ships to Xerxes’ fleet. Herodotus, from the same city, says she alone advised against fighting at Salamis, and that in the battle she escaped by ramming a ship from her own side. Seeing it, Xerxes is said to have remarked that his men had become women, and his women men.

items.name: Aeschylus
items.text: Aeschylus fought at Marathon, where his brother died, and probably at Salamis. His play The Persians, staged in 472 BCE with the young Pericles paying for the chorus, tells of Salamis from the Persian court. His epitaph names Marathon, not his plays. Of perhaps 70 to 90 plays, seven survive under his name.

items.name: Herodotus
items.text: Herodotus set out to record the great deeds of Greeks and non-Greeks, and why they fought. He travelled to Egypt, Babylon and the Black Sea and gathered stories from many peoples, some of them plainly legends. The Roman Cicero called him the father of history; others called him the father of lies. Much of this story rests on his Histories.

items.name: Pericles
items.text: Elected general year after year, Pericles led Athens at its height, building the Parthenon and backing the navy and the empire that paid for it. His speech for the war dead, as Thucydides gives it, calls Athens a school for all Greece. He died of the plague early in the war with Sparta.

items.name: Xenophon
items.text: A pupil of Socrates, Xenophon joined Cyrus the Younger’s army as a volunteer and became one of its leaders on the retreat; his Anabasis tells the story. Exiled from Athens, he lived on an estate near Olympia given by Sparta, and wrote on history, horsemanship, hunting and Cyrus the Great.

items.name: Mausolus
items.text: A Carian, Mausolus governed for the Persian king but acted as an independent ruler, moving his capital to Halicarnassus and rebuilding it as a Greek-style city with walls, a palace and harbours. He joined a revolt of satraps against Artaxerxes II and later backed Athens’ allies against it. His sister and wife, Artemisia II, ruled after him.

items.name: Philip II
items.text: As a teenage hostage in Thebes, Philip watched the best Greek army of the day. As king he built a professional army, took gold mines in Thrace, and used marriages and bribes as much as war. The Athenian Demosthenes warned against him in speeches still called philippics. His planned war on Persia passed to his son.

items.name: Alexander III, the Great
items.text: Taught by Aristotle, Alexander never lost a battle he commanded. In eleven years he took the Persian Empire and reached the Punjab, founding cities, many called Alexandria. He took up Persian dress and court customs, which angered many Macedonians. Whether he dreamt of uniting peoples or simply of conquest is still argued.

items.name: Darius III
items.text: Darius III came to the throne after the courtier Bagoas poisoned two kings; when Bagoas tried to poison him too, says Diodorus, Darius made him drink the cup himself. Greek writers, telling Alexander’s side, made him a coward for fleeing at Issus and Gaugamela. He was the last king of the Achaemenid line.

items.name: Sisygambis
items.text: Captured with Darius’s family at Issus, Sisygambis was treated by Alexander as a mother and travelled with his court. The Roman historian Curtius says that when she heard of Alexander’s death she refused food, and died five days later.

items.name: Spyridon Louis
items.text: Louis, who carried water into Athens from his village of Marousi, won the 1896 marathon by more than seven minutes, to the joy of the home crowd. He never raced again. At the 1936 Berlin Olympics he presented Hitler with an olive branch from Olympia. Athens’ Olympic stadium is named after him.
